question: A patient on phenelzine (irreversible MAOI) develops a severe hypertensive crisis after eating aged cheese. What is the pharmacological mechanism of this reaction?

answers.text: Dietary tyramine, normally metabolised by intestinal MAO-A, is absorbed intact and releases noradrenaline from sympathetic nerve terminals — causing a hypertensive crisis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Tyramine is an indirect sympathomimetic amine found in fermented/aged foods. Normally, MAO-A in the gut wall metabolises tyramine before it reaches the systemic circulation (first-pass). With MAO-A irreversibly inhibited by phenelzine, tyramine escapes first-pass metabolism, enters the circulation, and triggers massive noradrenaline release from sympathetic nerves → severe hypertension.

answers.text: Phenelzine directly stimulates α₁-adrenergic receptors in blood vessel walls, and cheese amplifies this effect

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Phenelzine does not directly stimulate adrenergic receptors. MAOIs work by inhibiting monoamine oxidase — they prevent the breakdown of monoamines. The hypertensive crisis is caused by tyramine (from cheese) releasing noradrenaline, not by direct receptor stimulation.

answers.text: Phenelzine inhibits CYP2D6, preventing hepatic tyramine metabolism and causing accumulation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The tyramine reaction involves MAO-A (in the gut wall and liver), not CYP2D6. Tyramine is a monoamine substrate for MAO — when MAO-A is inhibited, tyramine escapes first-pass metabolism and acts as an indirect sympathomimetic, releasing stored noradrenaline.

answers.text: Phenelzine blocks COMT, preventing adrenaline breakdown and causing a catecholamine surge when combined with dietary amines

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Phenelzine inhibits MAO (monoamine oxidase), not COMT. COMT inhibitors (entacapone, tolcapone) are used in Parkinson's disease. The tyramine reaction is specifically due to MAO-A inhibition in the gut wall allowing tyramine absorption intact.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the pathway: dietary tyramine → normally destroyed by gut MAO-A → with MAOI, tyramine reaches systemic circulation → enters sympathetic nerve terminals → displaces stored noradrenaline → massive NA release → hypertensive crisis.

The tyramine ('cheese') reaction occurs because MAO-A normally provides a first-pass metabolic barrier against dietary tyramine. Irreversible MAOIs remove this barrier — tyramine enters the circulation and triggers massive NA release. Moclobemide (reversible MAO-A inhibitor) is safer because tyramine can displace it from MAO-A.
